1.note: Here, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

2.note: The first instance of **you** (in **Send for you**) is singular and refers only to Moses. The second instance of **you** (in **you shall send**) is plural and refers to Moses and the Israelites. Use the appropriate singular or plural form of “you” in your language if your language marks that distinction.

Yahweh is using the present tense **am giving** to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to show that the event will happen soon. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Alternate translation: [I am about to give]

2.q: אִ֣ישׁ אֶחָד֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶחָ֜ד לְ⁠מַטֵּ֤ה אֲבֹתָי⁠ו֙
2.note: The phrase **one man, one man to the tribe of** is a common expression of this culture that means “one man for each tribe.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [One man for each tribe of]
God is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his ancestors]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people in the man’s tribe. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [among the people of his tribe]

3.note: The author is using the possessive form to describe a **wilderness** that is near **Paran**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 10:12. Alternate translation: [from the wilderness that was near Paran]

Here, **upon the mouth of Yahweh** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 9:23. Alternate translation: [according to what Yahweh commanded him]

Here, **heads** represents leaders. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar metaphor in 10:4. Alternate translation: [chiefs of]

4.note: Here and in 13:5–16, all the names are names of tribes or men.

8.note: The author assumes that readers will know that **Ephraim** was the son of Joseph, just as Manasseh was (see 13:11). You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for the tribe of Joseph, for the tribe of Ephraim]

11.note: The implication is that Manasseh was a subdivision of the larger tribe of Joseph. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for the tribe of Manasseh, which is part of the tribe of Joseph]

16.note: The author does not state directly when **Moses** did this. It could be: (1) at some earlier time. In this case, the author includes this information here to explain the name “Hoshea” in the list. Alternate translation: [and previously Moses had called] (2) at this time, when he sent the leaders to explore Canaan. Alternate translation: [and at that time Moses called]

The name **Hoshea** means “he saved.” The name **Joshua** means “Yahweh saved.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could give the meaning of these names in your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Hoshea (which means “he saved”), the son of Nun, Joshua (which means “Yahweh saved”)]

17.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֹתָ⁠ם֙ מֹשֶׁ֔ה לָ⁠ת֖וּר אֶת־אֶ֣רֶץ כְּנָ֑עַן וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר
17.note: The author is describing one event, **Moses sent them to explore the land of Canaan**, after already having described it in 13:3. If it would be helpful in your language, you may wish to relate these events in a different way to avoid repetition. Alternate translation: [And at the time when Moses sent them to explore the land of Canaan, he said]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Moses is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Go on … and you shall go to]
The pronoun **this** refers to the way ahead of them through the Negev. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [by the way in front of you] or [this way]

18.note: The implication is that Moses is asking about the land in general: its quality, characteristics, and suitability for settlement. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [what kind of place it is]

18.q: הֶ⁠חָזָ֥ק הוּא֙ הֲ⁠רָפֶ֔ה הַ⁠מְעַ֥ט ה֖וּא אִם־רָֽב
18.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the group of people living in the land. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [whether those people are strong or weak, whether those people are few or many]

19.note: By **what is the land**, Moses means what the land looks like and how people live in it. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and what are the features of the land]

The pronoun **it** refers to the people group who are living in the land that Moses told the men to explore. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those people are dwelling … those people are dwelling]

The implication is that the land could be good or bad for the people to live in. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [whether it is good to live in or bad to live in]

Here, Moses is speaking of unprotected settlements where people live as if they were **camps**, which were temporary settlements made of tents. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whether in unfortified towns]

20.note: The implication is that Moses wanted the spies to observe the quality of the soil itself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and what kind of ground it is]

The author is speaking of **the land** as if it were a living thing that could be fat or lean. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whether it can produce many crops or few crops]

Here, the phrase **strengthen yourselves** could mean that: (1) the leaders should work hard to do something. Alternate translation: [and you shall try hard to take] (2) the leaders should be courageous. Alternate translation: [and you shall be courageous, and you shall take]

In this verse, the word **fruit** is singular in form, but it refers to all the produce of the land as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “fruit.” Alternate translation: [from the fruits of the land]

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Now it is important to know that the days were the days of the firstfruits of the grapes]

The author is using the term **days** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it was the time of year for]

21.note: In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed this idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [And they went]
The words **Zin** and **Rehob** are the names of places. **Zin** refers to a wilderness area in the southern part of the land, and **Rehob** refers to a city in the northern part of the land.

Here, the phrase **Lebo Hamath** could be: (1) the name of a city which is near **Rehob**. Alternate translation: [up to Rehob, near the city of Lebo Hamath] (2) a phrase that refers to the entrance or way to a place called **Hamath**. Alternate translation: [up to Rehob, at the entrance to Hamath]

22.note: Here and in the following verses, the author provides the details of the travel that was summarized in 13:21. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate explicitly that the events in this and the following verses happened during the time described in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Specifically, they went up in the Negev] or [Here is how they did that. They went up in the Negev]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed this idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [And they went]

**Ahiman**, **Sheshai**, and **Talmai** could be the names of: (1) individual men. Alternate translation: [the men named Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai] (2) clans. Alternate translation: [the clans of Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai]

22.q: וְ⁠חֶבְר֗וֹן שֶׁ֤בַע שָׁנִים֙ נִבְנְתָ֔ה לִ⁠פְנֵ֖י צֹ֥עַן מִצְרָֽיִם
22.note: Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand what is happening in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [It is important to know that Hebron was built seven years to the face of Zoan, Egypt]

The expression **was built** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And its founders built Hebron]

The author is using the expression **to the face of** to mean “before” or “previous to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [prior to]
The words **Zoan** and **Egypt** are the names of a city and a country.

23.note: The word **Wadi Eshkol** is the name of a place. Here “Wadi” means a valley or streambed.

The phrase **branch and one cluster of grapes** expresses a single idea. The word **branch** tells more about the **cluster of grapes**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a branch with one cluster of grapes]

The author is not referring to a specific **carrying pole** that the reader knows about. He means any carrying pole. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [on a carrying pole]

The implication is that there were two men who carried the cluster of grapes. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with two men carrying it at a time]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they also took from the pomegranates and from the figs]

Here, **pomegranates** and **figs** represent these fruits in general, not specific ones. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and some pomegranates and some figs]

24.note: See how you translated the similar form in 11:3. Here, the pronoun **He** could refer: (1) generically to anyone who used this name. Alternate translation: [People called] (2) to Moses. Alternate translation: [Moses called]

The name **Eshkol** sounds like the Hebrew word for **cluster**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could make that explicit in your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Wadi Eshkol (which means “Cluster Wadi”) on account of the cluster]

25.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the 12 men who explored Canaan. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the 12 leaders returned]

26.note: It might seem that the expression **and they went and they came** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and they went] or [and they came]

The author is using the possessive form to describe a **congregation** that is made up of **the sons of Israel**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. See how you translated this phrase in 8:9. Alternate translation: [and to the congregation that consists of all the sons of Israel]

The implication is that the people of Israel were located in both the wilderness of Paran and specifically at the city of Kadesh when the scouts returned. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who were in the wilderness of Paran at Kadesh]

The phrase **returned them and all the congregation a word** is a common expression of this culture that means “gave them all a report” or “told them what they learned.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they told what they had learned to them and all the congregation]

The pronoun **they** refers to the 12 men who scouted out Canaan, the first pronoun **them** refers to Moses and Aaron, and the second pronoun **them** refers to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the 12 leaders returned Moses and Aaron … and the 12 leaders showed Moses, Aaron, and the congregation]

In this verse, the word **fruit** is singular in form, but it refers to all the produce as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “fruit.” See how you translated this phrase in 13:20. Alternate translation: [the fruits of]

27.note: The pronoun **him** refers to Moses. The men who explored Canaan spoke this report to Moses, but everyone else who was present also heard it. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to Moses publicly]

The term **and they said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

The phrase **where you sent us** shows that “us” refers to the 12 men who explored Canaan, but not to Moses, whom they are addressing, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, the author is speaking as if the land were actually **flowing with milk and honey**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it is rich and fertile] or [it is very productive]

In this verse, the word **fruit** is singular in form, but it refers to all the fruit (grapes, pomegranates, and figs) as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “fruit.” See how you translated this phrase in 13:20. Alternate translation: [and these are its fruits]

28.note: The expression **are fortified** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they have fortified their cities very greatly]
By **we saw**, the spies mean themselves but not Moses to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

29.note: Here, **Amalek** represents the Amalekite people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The Amalekites are dwelling]

29.q: וְ֠⁠הַֽ⁠חִתִּי וְ⁠הַ⁠יְבוּסִ֤י וְ⁠הָֽ⁠אֱמֹרִי֙ יוֹשֵׁ֣ב & וְ⁠הַֽ⁠כְּנַעֲנִי֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב
29.note: The men are not referring to specific **Hittite**, **Jebusite**, **Amorite**, and **Canaanite** people. They mean Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites, and Canaanites in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the Hittites and the Jebusites and the Amorites are dwelling … and the Canaanites are dwelling]

The author is using **upon the sea** as a common expression of his culture to mean “next to the sea” or “along the coast.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [next to the sea]

The author is using **upon the hand of the Jordan** as a common expression of his culture to mean “along the Jordan River.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and along the Jordan]

30.note: Here, the phrase **to Moses** could mean that Caleb hushed: (1) all the people who were assembled with Moses. Alternate translation: [who were assembled before Moses] (2) the people who were near Moses. Alternate translation: [near Moses]

30.q: עָלֹ֤ה נַעֲלֶה֙ וְ⁠יָרַ֣שְׁנוּ אֹתָ֔⁠הּ כִּֽי־יָכ֥וֹל נוּכַ֖ל לָֽ⁠הּ
30.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since **being able, we are able against it** gives the reason for the result that **going up, we will go up, and we will possess it** describes. Alternate translation: [Being able, we are able against it. So, going up, we will go up, and we will possess it]

The author is repeating forms of the verbs **go up** and **able** in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [We will certainly go up … for we are certainly able]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed the idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [Going, we will go]
By **we will go up … and we will possess it … we are able**, Caleb means to include both himself and his listeners, so use the inclusive form of those words if your language marks that distinction.

The pronoun **it** refers to the land that the Israelites will possess and go up against. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and we will possess the land … against the land]

Caleb is using **we are able against it** as a common expression of his culture to mean “we are able to conquer it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are able to conquer it]

31.note: In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. See how you expressed the idea in 13:17. Alternate translation: [went]

31.q: לֹ֥א נוּכַ֖ל לַ⁠עֲל֣וֹת אֶל־הָ⁠עָ֑ם כִּֽי־חָזָ֥ק ה֖וּא מִמֶּֽ⁠נּוּ
31.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since **it is stronger than us** gives the reason for the result that **we are not able to go up against the people** describes. Alternate translation: [The people is stronger than us, so we are not able to go up against it]
By **us**, the men who went up with Caleb mean themselves and the rest of the Israelites, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The spies are using **to go up against the people** as a common expression of their culture to mean “to fight against” or “to defeat.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to fight against the people] or [to defeat the people]
The pronoun **it** refers to the people of Canaan. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those people are stronger]

32.note: Here, the scouts are speaking as if a **report** were an object that could be **brought out**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they gave a bad report]

32.q: הָ⁠אָ֡רֶץ אֲשֶׁר֩ עָבַ֨רְנוּ בָ֜⁠הּ לָ⁠ת֣וּר אֹתָ֗⁠הּ אֶ֣רֶץ אֹכֶ֤לֶת יוֹשְׁבֶ֨י⁠הָ֙ הִ֔וא
32.note: It might seem that the expression **it is a land** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [The land through which we passed to explore it eats the ones dwelling in it]

By **we passed**, the spies mean themselves but not Moses and the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here, the spies speak as if the land were a person that could eat the people who live there. Some scholars think this refers to a specific danger, like famine or war. However, it is recommended that you refer generally to dangers that people would experience living in the land. Alternate translation: [a land that is as dangerous as if it ate the ones dwelling in it] or [a land that is dangerous for the ones dwelling in it]

The author is using the possessive form to describe **men** that are characterized by **size**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sizable men] or [large men]

Here the masculine term **men of** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [humans of]

33.note: By **we**, the spies mean to include themselves but not Moses and the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your language if your language marks that distinction.

Here, the author is providing background information to help readers understand the identity of **the sons of Anak**. He interrupts the quote to do so. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [it is important to know that the sons of Anak are from the Nephils]

Here, the author is speaking as if the people of the tribes descended from Anak were actually his **sons**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those descended from Anak]

Here, the phrase **from the Nephils** could mean: (1) that the sons of Anak are **Nephils**. Alternate translation: [are a type of Nephil] (2) that the sons of Anak are descended from **Nephils**. Alternate translation: [are descended from the Nephils]

Here, **eyes** represents what people thought or perceived about themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in our sight … in their sight] or [in our perception … in their perception]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grasshoppers** are small and insignificant compared to humans, so the Israelite spies felt small and insignificant compared to the people of Canaan. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as small and insignificant as grasshoppers]

A **grasshopper** is a kind of jumping insect. If your readers would not be familiar with what a grasshopper is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like the small jumping insects]

The men are not referring to specific **grasshoppers**. They mean grasshoppers in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like grasshoppers]
